RRI Encyclopedia Steliu Lambru , 03.10.2026, 14:00 Forensic medicine is the branch of medicine that makes it easier to establish the truth and ensures that the law is applied fairly. The institutional history of forensic medicine in Romania began in the second half of the 19th century, following the formation of the Romanian state in 1859 and the emergence of specialists trained at higher education institutions in the West. There are several names that stand out in the history of Romanian forensic medicine, with those of brothers Mina and Nicolae Minovici being essential. The two wrote pages of genuine medical heroism, earning the respect of both their contemporaries and posterity. The year 1892 marks the establishment of the first institute of forensic medicine in Bucharest. The Minovici brothers were of Aromanian origin, born in what is now North Macedonia, and came from a wealthy family. All three brothers were born in Romania: the first two, Mina in 1858 and Ștefan in 1867, in Brăila, while the third, Nicolae, was born in 1868 in Râmnicu Sărat. All three studied medicine, but only the first and third devoted themselves to forensic medicine. Mina Minovici, the eldest, specialised in toxicology and became an assistant to Carol Davila at the School of Medicine and Pharmacy, founded by Davila himself. Dr Octavian Buda is a psychiatrist at the “Mina Minovici” National Institute of Legal Medicine in Bucharest and a professor of medical history at the “Carol Davila” University of Medicine and Pharmacy in Bucharest. He told us about the relationship that developed between Mina Minovici and Carol Davila: “Mina Minovici had a very amusing memory of Carol Davila, who also carried out biochemical experiments and explained the various chemical reactions that took place. One of the challenges of 19th-century toxicology, as it is today, was identifying substances that caused poisoning when a doctor performed an autopsy on a corpse. At one point, Davila wanted to demonstrate that, for example, printing ink was not affected by chlorine gas. He took the newspaper Românul and put it into the chlorine-filled vessel, at which point the Frenchman Carol Davila told them: ‘Gentlemen, here you have proof that the Romanian does not perish even in chlorine!’ Carol Davila was a more direct, hot-tempered, even somewhat aggressive man, and he managed, initially, to set up a kind of post-secondary medical school.” Although healers and doctors had been important in every type of human society, the importance of doctors in a developing Romania was becoming even greater. Forensic doctors, in turn, were becoming highly important within the architecture of the state and in the decisions being made. Octavian Buda: “One very important aspect concerns the way health measures were taken at urban level. In other words, forensic doctors contributed to public health policies in the city and were, of course, highly respected. They even had a say in matters related to the outbreak of epidemics at local level. Cholera, for example, was a major problem for the pathology of the time, and forensic doctors certainly had a role to play.” Mina Minovici returned to Romania, where he found an atmosphere of intellectual emulation and favourable conditions for developing his discipline. Octavian Buda: “Minovici was interested, for example, in the problem of identifying substances that caused poisoning and suspicious deaths. In fact, as early as 1886-87, he already had the training that would later enable him to return to Bucharest and insist, with some determination, on the establishment of an institute of forensic medicine. Autopsies were being carried out in Bucharest, at Colțea Hospital and at Brâncovenesc Hospital. Two very serious and distinguished men were Alexandru Suțu, who came from the family of the Phanariot rulers and who was also trained in forensic medicine and psychiatry, and a Bulgarian, Gheorghe Atanasovici. He, too, taught forensic medicine in Bucharest, after which he went to Sofia and also held important political positions. He was a very well-known and highly respected figure in Bulgaria, but, interestingly enough, he first taught forensic medicine in Bucharest.” The third Minovici brother, Nicolae, also became famous for the self-hanging experiment to which he subjected himself. Octavian Buda: “There are neurological aspects related to the deprivation of oxygen to the brain at the moment of strangulation. He was interested in the following: first of all, whether a person who is hanged struggles before the final moments, and whether it is possible to distinguish between someone who was murdered and then placed in a noose. There are certain characteristics. Unfortunately, there is also a very bizarre category of autoerotic accidents involving hanging. He was interested in this aspect as well: what happens in such cases? What are the mental and psychiatric states of those found dead, hanged in such circumstances? He wanted to examine, precisely, a kind of psychopathology of hanging. Obviously, the experiment was conducted under controlled conditions. In other words, he recorded every step, every second, and described in great detail what he felt. Nicolae Minovici is truly the prototype of a forensic doctor, in the fullest sense of the word. Mina Minovici was more of a toxicologist. Of course, Mina performed autopsies and practised forensic medicine, but he was something of a chemist who had turned to forensic medicine. Nicolae Minovici, the youngest of the three brothers, was also the smallest in stature and the most energetic. His first paper on forensic medicine was actually entitled The Technique of Autopsy.” The rich history of Romanian forensic medicine is also on display in museums. A hatóságok még tavaly fedezték fel, hogy a Megaspeed ötvenezerrel több chipet importált annál, mint amennyit az Nvidia ellenőrei a vállalat szingapúri adatközpontjaiban ténylegesen megtaláltak. Egy névtelenséget kérő volt minisztériumi tisztviselő szerint a tárcánál már 2025 nyarán tudtak a Megaspeeddel kapcsolatos súlyos problémákról. A szakértők ekkoriban dolgoztak egy új szabályozáson, amely exportengedélyhez kötötte volna a fejlett chipek értékesítését bizonyos délkelet-ázsiai országokba. Bár a tervezetet 2025 júliusára minden érintett ügynökség jóváhagyta, és a bevezetésével jelentősen korlátozni lehetett volna a Megaspeedhez hasonló cégek chipbeszerzéseit, Howard Lutnick miniszter nem volt hajlandó kihirdetni a rendeletet. A mulasztás miatt kétpárti kongresszusi vizsgálat indulhat Lutnick, valamint az exportkorlátozásokat felügyelő Ipari és Biztonsági Hivatal (BIS) vezetője, Jeffrey Kessler ellen. A késlekedés a kormányzaton belül is komoly feszültséget szült, így Scott Bessent pénzügyminiszter személyesen vonta kérdőre Lutnicket, a Reuters értesülései szerint pedig a Fehér Házban már a miniszter menesztését is fontolgatják, bár hivatalosan továbbra is Donald Trump elnök teljes bizalmáról biztosították őt. A kritikák kereszttüzébe került a Kessler és az Nvidia közötti kommunikáció is, miután kiderült, hogy a chipgyártó vezető jogtanácsosa közvetlenül nála érdeklődött Alice Huang 2025-ös szingapúri őrizetbe vételéről, ami után a minisztériumi dolgozókat eltiltották a cég önálló vizsgálatától. A hivatal szóvivője ugyanakkor alaptalannak nevezte a vádakat, hangsúlyozva, hogy Kessler végig a szabályoknak megfelelően és pártatlanul járt el. A botrány kirobbanásával párhuzamosan a kereskedelmi tárca most egy új rendelet véglegesítésén dolgozik, amely hét délkelet-ázsiai országra – köztük Szingapúrra, Malajziára és Thaiföldre – terjesztené ki az exportkorlátozásokat. Az intézkedés célja, hogy bezárja azt a kiskaput, amelyen keresztül a kínai vállalatok távoli hozzáféréssel használhatják az ezekben az országokban működő adatközpontok Nvidia-chipjeit. Photograph: Martin Pope/Getty Images Immigration and asylum Suffolk village votes to ‘leave the UK’ over plans to house asylum seekers nearby Local MP says legitimate criticisms of asylum housing plans are being co-opted by opposition parties ‘stirring up racial discord’ Harry Cockburn Sat 21 Nov 2026 13.20 EST Last modified on Sat 21 Nov 2026 14.01 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Residents of a Suffolk village have voted to “leave the UK” in a referendum held in response to government plans to house 930 asylum seekers at a nearby former military base. Approximately 500 people in Barnham were eligible to take part in the symbolic vote on Saturday. There were 257 votes for independence, 16 against and one spoiled ballot. After the vote, Helen Beck, the chair of Barnham Residents’ Association, said Barnham’s flag would be a stone-curlew on a “Suffolk blue background”. RAF Barnham was one of three Ministry of Defence sites named in June by the government as potential locations for new developments to house asylum seekers. View image in fullscreen The flag of Barnham’s mooted new crown dependency, featuring a stone-curlew against a ‘Suffolk blue background’. Photograph: Martin Pope/Getty Images A similar referendum was held in Piddington, Oxfordshire in September, with residents also voting to leave the UK amid plans to house more than 1,000 migrants at another former military base. In Barnham, the plans have prompted protests outside the site. The referendum asked residents whether they supported seeking a “crown dependency status”, which is a similar system to that of Jersey, Guernsey and the Isle of Man. John Bauer, the parish council chair, said this would allow the village to “retain loyalty to the crown” but remove itself from Home Office jurisdiction. While in opposition the Labour party had attacked the Conservative policy to house asylum seekers on military bases; once in government, however, the party backtracked. The Conservatives have also reversed their position, with Kemi Badenoch telling frustrated villagers “the Conservative party is on your side”. “We know that the problem of the boats needs to stop and we have got a plan to stop it,” she said on Friday. Earlier this month, it was announced construction company Kier would design the new camp at RAF Barnham. Before Saturday’s vote Labour’s Dr Peter Prinsley, the local MP, said he was against the development of the site. Prinsley said the plans resembled a “concentration camp”, and warned that planning permission may be difficult to attain due to environmental concerns about rare species living in the area – in particular, stone-curlews – with previous development applications nearby having been turned down. “This is a symbolic referendum,” Prinsley said. “It’s not going to produce a binding result. I’m expecting that [the result] will be hugely in favour of becoming a crown dependency. There are 500 electors, so I’m expecting it to be 500 – nil.” He added that the government “is doing an awful lot to deal with the irregular migration problem”, and highlighted that net migration may come down to “more or less zero by the end of the year”. But he added that he didn’t think “the large army camps in remote locations are ever likely to be appropriate for the distribution of people seeking asylum. The fact is that people who arrive here on small boats are not illegal migrants. They are people who are seeking asylum. Our political opponents have described these people as ‘illegals, criminals, rapists’, and all sorts of things that they’re not. They’re just people who have arrived on small boats. The government is getting a grip on this problem, but it’s a complicated problem.” He said the proposed Barnham site had particular issues which may make it unsuitable. “It’s a remote location without any pedestrian access, it’s on a very hazardous main road. When it was used as military accommodation there were serious accidents on that road. “It’s also a site of special scientific interest because it is the nesting site for stone-curlews, which will make any planning application very difficult – even a government planning application – because these are worldwide protections.” He suggested “disused office blocks in some of the larger cities” may be more appropriate places to house asylum seekers, with more local services available. View image in fullscreen The permanent protest camp outside the gates of the former RAF base where the Home Office propose to house asylum seekers. Photograph: Martin Pope/Getty Images “It feels like a concentration camp,” Prinsley added. “It doesn’t feel like a place that has a compassionate approach to people who are fleeing persecution and are being processed for asylum.” He also said legitimate criticism of the plans had been co-opted by opposition parties who are aiming to “stir up racial discord”. A Home Office spokesperson said: “We recognise the strength of feeling in local communities and are listening carefully to the concerns being raised. “The government is working on a fairer distribution of asylum accommodation across the country, with over £1bn saved in costs since the election. “This includes closing all asylum hotels and moving to alternative accommodation, including former military sites. These are designed to be self-contained, with 24/7 security and CCTV, to reduce the impact on local communities.” Explore more on these topics Immigration and asylum England Migration Communities Suffolk Home Office news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland
